{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_01NmB18FFCrPbYt1sxhWRVgQ","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# AI / agentic layer — detail\n2\t\n3\tLoad this when Step 1 classifies the system as AI or agentic. The order below is deliberate:\n4\tdefenses and budgets are built BEFORE capabilities, because an unguarded or unmetered agent\n5\tis a liability the moment it touches real input or real money.\n6\t\n7\t## Defenses and budgets (build first)\n8\t\n9\t### 1. Prompt-injection / guardrail defense\n10\tUntrusted input (user text, retrieved documents, tool output) can carry instructions. Treat\n11\tall of it as data, never as commands. Concrete moves:\n12\t- Separate system/trusted instructions from untrusted content at the API boundary.\n13\t- Input and output filters (PII, jailbreak patterns, disallowed content).\n14\t- Constrain tool calls to an allow-list; validate arguments before execution.\n15\t- Exit check: a known injection string in a retrieved doc does not change agent behavior.\n16\t\n17\t### 2. Cost + latency budget\n18\tAn agent loop can spend unbounded tokens and time. Set budgets before capability:\n19\t- Per-request token cap, per-session cost cap, max tool-call / reasoning iterations.\n20\t- A latency budget with a timeout and a graceful degraded response.\n21\t- Exit check: a runaway loop is cut off at the cap and emits a cost/latency metric.\n22\t\n23\t### 3. Human-in-the-loop gating\n24\tDecide which actions require a human before they execute (writes, spend, external messages,\n25\tirreversible operations). Low-risk reads run autonomously; high-blast-radius actions gate.\n26\t- Exit check: a gated action pauses for approval and is auditable.\n27\t\n28\t## Capability order (build after defenses)\n29\t\n30\t### 4. Retrieval\n31\tGet the right context in. Chunking, embeddings, index, and relevance evaluation.\n32\t- Exit check: for a known query, the expected source passages are retrieved.\n33\t\n34\t### 5. Model access\n35\tA thin, swappable interface to the model(s): provider abstraction, retries, fallback model,\n36\tstructured-output parsing.\n37\t- Exit check: the model can be swapped via config without touching call sites.\n38\t\n39\t### 6. Memory\n40\tWhat persists across turns/sessions: short-term conversation state and long-term store, with\n41\tan explicit write policy and a privacy boundary.\n42\t- Exit check: relevant prior context is recalled; stale/forbidden data is not written.\n43\t\n44\t### 7. Orchestration\n45\tHow steps compose: single call, chain, or multi-agent. Keep it the simplest shape that works.\n46\t- Exit check: a multi-step task completes end-to-end with each step traced.\n47\t\n48\t### 8. Routing\n49\tSend each request to the right model/tool/path by difficulty, cost, or capability.\n50\t- Exit check: cheap requests take the cheap path; hard ones escalate, both logged.\n51\t\n52\t### 9. Feedback\n53\tCapture outcomes (thumbs, corrections, eval scores) and route them back into prompts,\n54\tretrieval tuning, or training data.\n55\t- Exit check: a captured correction measurably changes a later response or an eval metric.\n56\t\n57\t## Notes\n58\t- Every sublayer still obeys the cross-cutting columns (security, observability,\n59\t  reproducibility, resilience). Observability here means per-step traces, token/cost metrics,\n60\t  and eval scores — from day zero.\n61\t- Prefer prompt+RAG over fine-tuning until a Tradeoff gate's flip condition is met; it is the\n62\t  less rigid, more reversible choice (SKILL principle 2).\n63\t"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"e78497f9-53ac-435a-9d40-aec82120643e","uuid":"42a2b246-c42b-4174-8169-8c355f593b5b","timestamp":"2026-10-03T00:28:12.251Z","tool_use_result":{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"C:\\Users\\nrvhari\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\dfa-eval\\2026-10-03-pilot-core\\plugins\\p1f4bc0e3\\skills\\dependency-first-architect\\reference\\ai-systems.md","content":"# AI / agentic layer — detail\n\nLoad this when Step 1 classifies the system as AI or agentic. The order below is deliberate:\ndefenses and budgets are built BEFORE capabilities, because an unguarded or unmetered agent\nis a liability the moment it touches real input or real money.\n\n## Defenses and budgets (build first)\n\n### 1. Prompt-injection / guardrail defense\nUntrusted input (user text, retrieved documents, tool output) can carry instructions. Treat\nall of it as data, never as commands. Concrete moves:\n- Separate system/trusted instructions from untrusted content at the API boundary.\n- Input and output filters (PII, jailbreak patterns, disallowed content).\n- Constrain tool calls to an allow-list; validate arguments before execution.\n- Exit check: a known injection string in a retrieved doc does not change agent behavior.\n\n### 2. Cost + latency budget\nAn agent loop can spend unbounded tokens and time. Set budgets before capability:\n- Per-request token cap, per-session cost cap, max tool-call / reasoning iterations.\n- A latency budget with a timeout and a graceful degraded response.\n- Exit check: a runaway loop is cut off at the cap and emits a cost/latency metric.\n\n### 3. Human-in-the-loop gating\nDecide which actions require a human before they execute (writes, spend, external messages,\nirreversible operations). Low-risk reads run autonomously; high-blast-radius actions gate.\n- Exit check: a gated action pauses for approval and is auditable.\n\n## Capability order (build after defenses)\n\n### 4. Retrieval\nGet the right context in. Chunking, embeddings, index, and relevance evaluation.\n- Exit check: for a known query, the expected source passages are retrieved.\n\n### 5. Model access\nA thin, swappable interface to the model(s): provider abstraction, retries, fallback model,\nstructured-output parsing.\n- Exit check: the model can be swapped via config without touching call sites.\n\n### 6. Memory\nWhat persists across turns/sessions: short-term conversation state and long-term store, with\nan explicit write policy and a privacy boundary.\n- Exit check: relevant prior context is recalled; stale/forbidden data is not written.\n\n### 7. Orchestration\nHow steps compose: single call, chain, or multi-agent. Keep it the simplest shape that works.\n- Exit check: a multi-step task completes end-to-end with each step traced.\n\n### 8. Routing\nSend each request to the right model/tool/path by difficulty, cost, or capability.\n- Exit check: cheap requests take the cheap path; hard ones escalate, both logged.\n\n### 9. Feedback\nCapture outcomes (thumbs, corrections, eval scores) and route them back into prompts,\nretrieval tuning, or training data.\n- Exit check: a captured correction measurably changes a later response or an eval metric.\n\n## Notes\n- Every sublayer still obeys the cross-cutting columns (security, observability,\n  reproducibility, resilience). Observability here means per-step traces, token/cost metrics,\n  and eval scores — from day zero.\n- Prefer prompt+RAG over fine-tuning until a Tradeoff gate's flip condition is met; it is the\n  less rigid, more reversible choice (SKILL principle 2).\n","numLines":63,"startLine":1,"totalLines":63}}}

Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\nThe thinnest end-to-end path that runs in production:\n- The one real request and the real response.\n- Every tier it crosses.\n- How it is deployed, logged, and monitored on day zero.\nExit check: a real request returns a real response in prod, with a trace and a metric visible.\n\n## 4. Phases (ordered by dependency; within a phase, widest blast radius first)\nFor each phase:\n- **Phase N — <name>**\n  - Unlocks: what becomes possible after it.\n  - Depends on: the proven thing it builds on.\n  - Tasks: ordered widest-blast-radius → narrowest.\n  - Exit check: the observable condition that proves the phase is done.\n\n## 5. Cross-cutting concerns (per phase, from the first commit)\nA table with one row per phase and columns for the concrete move made in each:\n\n| Phase | Security | Observability | Reproducibility | Resilience |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 0 | … | … | … | … |\n\nObservability appears in Phase 0. None of these columns may be empty.\n\n## 6. AI layer (AI/agentic systems only)\nDefenses/budgets first, then capability order:\n1. Prompt-injection / guardrail defense\n2. Cost + latency budget\n3. Human-in-the-loop gating\n4. Retrieval\n5. Model access\n6. Memory\n7. Orchestration\n8. Routing\n9. Feedback\n\nFor each: what it is in THIS system, and its exit check. Omit this section for non-AI systems.\n\n## 7. Deliberately deferred\nBullet list: what you are NOT building yet, and the condition that pulls each item forward.\n\n## 8. Eval score\nReport the self-score against `reference/evals.md` as **/20**, with a one-line note per\nrubric dimension. If below 16, revise above and re-score before delivering.\n","numLines":72,"startLine":1,"totalLines":72}}}

{"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-5-5","id":"msg_bdrk_bjihna2sp54denwfb55l3pjcoitkknda6wbsdmh7reev7fstt5eq","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"# BUILD PLAN: Real-time card-transaction fraud detection\n\n**Assumptions** (any of these can be overridden):\n- We are the issuer or processor, and we score each authorization inline before it is approved.\n- An authorization switch already exists, along with an incumbent control (network scores and/or legacy rules).\n- Traffic is a mix of card-present and card-not-present.\n- The switch gives us **≤100 ms** to score. This is the first number to confirm in Phase 0.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Classification\n- **What:** A service that scores each card authorization for fraud within the auth-path latency budget and returns approve, step-up, review or decline. Behind it sit a streaming feature pipeline, a label (ground-truth) pipeline and a retraining loop.\n- **Type:** A mix of software and infra, plus classical ML (gradient-boosted trees). It is **not** generative or agentic AI.\n- **Dominant constraint:** **Latency.** It is a hard p99 limit inside the auth path. Correctness (fraud caught vs. good customers declined) and compliance (PCI DSS v4.0, model risk governance) come close behind.\n- **Worst failure:** The scorer sits in the auth path, and a bad deploy, bad model or dependency outage causes **mass false declines**, or it **fails open silently** so fraud passes while every dashboard looks green. The design has to make both failures impossible to miss and limited in scope.\n\n## 2. Tradeoff gates (resolved up front)\n\n| Decision | Default (chosen now) | Flip condition |\n|---|---|---|\n| Consistency vs availability | **Availability on the scoring path.** Feature reads may be up to about 2 s stale (velocity counters are eventually consistent). **Strong consistency for the decision log:** every decision is durably recorded and replayable. | Card-testing or burst attacks start exploiting the staleness window, i.e. measurable losses from transactions that fell inside it. Then switch to single-writer, strongly consistent per-card counters (partitioned by card token). |\n| Monolith vs services | **Two deployables, split by latency class.** (1) An inline scoring service: a modular monolith holding rules, model and decision policy. (2) An async streaming and feature pipeline. Nothing finer-grained. | Separate teams need independent release cycles for rules vs. model, or rules evaluation needs to scale independently. |\n| Sync vs async | **Sync only for the decision.** Everything else is async through Kafka: feature updates, decision logging, case creation, labels, retraining. | The inline model can't hold p99 within budget at peak. Then keep rules inline and move the model to near-real-time post-auth scoring, which triggers alerts and blocks the card for the *next* transaction. |\n| **Failure mode** (fail-open vs fail-closed) | **Fail to the existing fallback.** On timeout or error the switch uses incumbent rules plus network stand-in. If those are also unavailable, approve below a per-MCC amount ceiling and decline above it. Never fail closed globally. | Risk appetite changes (e.g. a regulator or loss event) and someone formally accepts a fail-closed policy for specific segments. |\n| Build vs buy | **Buy the infra, build the decisioning.** Managed Kafka (MSK or Confluent), managed Flink, Redis/ElastiCache (or Aerospike), Iceberg on S3 and MLflow. Build features, rules, model and policy in house. Network scores (Visa VAA, Mastercard Decision Intelligence) go in as *features*. | After 6 months of shadow testing, the in-house model doesn't beat the incumbent plus network score at the same decline rate, or the team is too small to run on-call. Then buy a vendor scorer (Featurespace, Feedzai) and keep the substrate. |\n| Feature computation model | **One feature definition, streaming first.** The same Flink logic writes the online store and is replayed for offline backfill, so training and serving cannot drift apart. | Replaying history becomes too expensive (e.g. a full backfill takes more than 24 h). Then add a batch path that is checked by an automated online/offline comparison. |\n| Model family | **GBDT (LightGBM/XGBoost).** CPU inference under 5 ms, SHAP reason codes, defensible for model-risk review. | A sequence or graph model shows material recall lift at a fixed false-positive rate in shadow testing *and* fits the latency budget. |\n| (ML) Hosted model API vs in-process | **In-process inference**, using a Treelite/ONNX artifact embedded in the scorer. There is no network hop and no third-party API in the auth path. | Model size or GPU needs exceed what the scorer pods can hold. Then use a co-located sidecar, still never a remote API. |\n| (AI) Prompt+RAG vs fine-tune | **N/A.** No LLM is in the decision path. | Revisit if an LLM analyst copilot is pulled forward (see §7). |\n| Data-privacy / PCI boundary | **PAN is tokenized before it reaches the scorer.** The fraud system sees only token, BIN and last-4, which keeps it out of the cardholder-data environment (CDE) where possible. | A feature truly needs raw PAN (rare, since BIN covers most needs). That part then enters PCI scope with a separate CDE segment. |\n\n## 3. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n\n**The one real request:** a live production authorization goes from the auth switch to the scorer. The scorer returns `{decision, score, reason_codes, rule_version, model_version}`. It runs **inline but non-enforcing**: the switch logs our answer and keeps its own decision. This is the only safe way to get the real latency figure on day one.\n\n**Tiers crossed:**\n1. **Auth switch**: a new client call with a **30 ms hard timeout** and a circuit breaker, behind a feature flag with a traffic % dial (1% → 100%).\n2. **Scoring service** (gRPC, Kubernetes, 2 availability zones), with a minimal canonical request schema v0.\n3. **Online store** (Redis): read one feature, the card token's count of transactions in the last hour.\n4. **Decision**: one hard-coded velocity rule (e.g. more than 10 auths per hour means \"would decline\") and a constant model placeholder.\n5. **Event bus**: the decision event goes to Kafka through a non-blocking producer with a bounded local buffer, so the hot path never waits on Kafka.\n6. **Stream processor**: a Flink job consumes transaction events, updates the Redis velocity counter and sinks decisions to an Iceberg decision log.\n7. **Dashboard**: Grafana.\n\n**Deploy:** Terraform for infra. CI builds an image pinned by digest. GitOps (Argo CD) rolls it out. The switch flag starts at 1%.\n\n**Logged and monitored from day zero:**\n- An OpenTelemetry trace ID is carried from the switch through the scorer and Redis, into the Kafka header, and on to Flink.\n- Metrics: p50/p99/p99.9 latency, timeout rate, would-decline rate, Kafka consumer lag, and Redis error rate.\n- Alerts: p99 > 30 ms, timeout rate > 0.1%, would-decline rate moving ±3σ from baseline, consumer lag > 30 s.\n\n**Exit check:** 100% of production auths traverse the path. One transaction can be followed end to end in a single trace, from switch through scorer to Redis to Kafka to Flink to Iceberg. Real p99 is measured and confirmed under budget. Killing the scorer pods causes **zero** change to auth outcomes, which proves the fallback works.\n\n## 4. Phases (ordered by dependency; within each phase, widest blast radius first)\n\n**Phase 1: Data contracts and event substrate**\n- Unlocks: every feature, label and model downstream. They all depend on these schemas and entity keys.\n- Depends on: Phase 0's proven path (schema v0 and the real event flow).\n- Tasks:\n  1. **Entity identity model** (widest blast radius): card token, account, customer, merchant ID + MCC, device/fingerprint, and how they join.\n  2. Canonical `TransactionEvent`, `DecisionEvent` and `LabelEvent` schemas in Protobuf with a schema registry. Backward-compatibility checks are enforced in CI.\n  3. Event-time semantics: timestamps and a late/out-of-order policy (watermarks, e.g. 5 s allowed lateness).\n  4. Sliding vs. tumbling windows, and the key per window. Every feature inherits these.\n  2. Online store SLO: p99 read < 5 ms, sized for 3× peak traffic per second.\n  3. What counts as fraud: chargeback reason codes, confirmed customer disputes, analyst dispositions. Chargebacks arrive 30–120 days late, so labels mature at 90 days.\n  2. Ingestion from the chargeback, dispute and case systems.\n  3. Selection-bias accounting: declined transactions have no outcome, so they are flagged and handled in evaluation.\n  4. Fallback chain is formalized and tested: scorer → incumbent rules → network stand-in → MCC amount ceiling.\n  3. Rules engine: rules are versioned config in git, hot-reloaded and signed, with a per-rule kill switch.\n  4. Model registry (MLflow) with signed artifacts and a model card for model-risk review.\n  4. In-process serving integration, held under the latency budget.\n  5. Shadow scoring on 100% of traffic, then a champion/challenger traffic split.\n- Exit check: on matured labels, the model beats rules alone at an equal decline rate. AI layer\n**N/A as defined (no LLM, no agent).** This is a classical ML system, so the LLM-specific sublayers do not apply: prompt-injection defense, retrieval, LLM memory, orchestration and routing. Deliberately deferred\n- **Graph and fraud-ring features (or a GNN).** Pull forward when ring or mule fraud exceeds about 15% of losses.\n- **Deep sequence models.** Pull forward when GBDT recall plateaus across two retrains and a shadow test shows material lift within budget.\n- **Online or continuous learning.** Pull forward when attack adaptation outpaces the daily retrain (loss spikes before the next model ships).\n- **Strongly consistent per-card counters.** Pull forward on the consistency gate's flip condition.\n- **Bought feature-store product (Feast/Tecton).** Pull forward when there are more than about 100 features or more than one team producing features.\n- **Self-serve rules UI for fraud ops.** Pull forward when rule changes exceed about 10 per week and pull-request review becomes the bottleneck.\n- **Exploration holdout** (letting a tiny, capped sample of would-be declines through to measure true outcomes). Pull forward when selection bias measurably distorts evaluation, and only with risk sign-off.\n- **LLM analyst copilot** (case summarization). Pull forward when analyst throughput is the binding constraint. This is the first number to confirm in Phase 0.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Classification\n- **What:** A service that scores each card authorization for fraud within the auth-path latency budget and returns approve, step-up, review or decline. Behind it sit a streaming feature pipeline, a label (ground-truth) pipeline and a retraining loop.\n- **Type:** A mix of software and infra, plus classical ML (gradient-boosted trees). It is **not** generative or agentic AI.\n- **Dominant constraint:** **Latency.** It is a hard p99 limit inside the auth path. Correctness (fraud caught vs. good customers declined) and compliance (PCI DSS v4.0, model risk governance) come close behind.\n- **Worst failure:** The scorer sits in the auth path, and a bad deploy, bad model or dependency outage causes **mass false declines**, or it **fails open silently** so fraud passes while every dashboard looks green. The design has to make both failures impossible to miss and limited in scope.\n\n## 2. Tradeoff gates (resolved up front)\n\n| Decision | Default (chosen now) | Flip condition |\n|---|---|---|\n| Consistency vs availability | **Availability on the scoring path.** Feature reads may be up to about 2 s stale (velocity counters are eventually consistent). **Strong consistency for the decision log:** every decision is durably recorded and replayable. | Card-testing or burst attacks start exploiting the staleness window, i.e. measurable losses from transactions that fell inside it. Then switch to single-writer, strongly consistent per-card counters (partitioned by card token). |\n| Monolith vs services | **Two deployables, split by latency class.** (1) An inline scoring service: a modular monolith holding rules, model and decision policy. (2) An async streaming and feature pipeline. Nothing finer-grained. | Separate teams need independent release cycles for rules vs. model, or rules evaluation needs to scale independently. |\n| Sync vs async | **Sync only for the decision.** Everything else is async through Kafka: feature updates, decision logging, case creation, labels, retraining. | The inline model can't hold p99 within budget at peak. Then keep rules inline and move the model to near-real-time post-auth scoring, which triggers alerts and blocks the card for the *next* transaction. |\n| **Failure mode** (fail-open vs fail-closed) | **Fail to the existing fallback.** On timeout or error the switch uses incumbent rules plus network stand-in. If those are also unavailable, approve below a per-MCC amount ceiling and decline above it. Never fail closed globally. | Risk appetite changes (e.g. a regulator or loss event) and someone formally accepts a fail-closed policy for specific segments. |\n| Build vs buy | **Buy the infra, build the decisioning.** Managed Kafka (MSK or Confluent), managed Flink, Redis/ElastiCache (or Aerospike), Iceberg on S3 and MLflow. Build features, rules, model and policy in house. Network scores (Visa VAA, Mastercard Decision Intelligence) go in as *features*. | After 6 months of shadow testing, the in-house model doesn't beat the incumbent plus network score at the same decline rate, or the team is too small to run on-call. Then buy a vendor scorer (Featurespace, Feedzai) and keep the substrate. |\n| Feature computation model | **One feature definition, streaming first.** The same Flink logic writes the online store and is replayed for offline backfill, so training and serving cannot drift apart. | Replaying history becomes too expensive (e.g. a full backfill takes more than 24 h). Then add a batch path that is checked by an automated online/offline comparison. |\n| Model family | **GBDT (LightGBM/XGBoost).** CPU inference under 5 ms, SHAP reason codes, defensible for model-risk review. | A sequence or graph model shows material recall lift at a fixed false-positive rate in shadow testing *and* fits the latency budget. |\n| (ML) Hosted model API vs in-process | **In-process inference**, using a Treelite/ONNX artifact embedded in the scorer. There is no network hop and no third-party API in the auth path. | Model size or GPU needs exceed what the scorer pods can hold. Then use a co-located sidecar, still never a remote API. |\n| (AI) Prompt+RAG vs fine-tune | **N/A.** No LLM is in the decision path. | Revisit if an LLM analyst copilot is pulled forward (see §7). |\n| Data-privacy / PCI boundary | **PAN is tokenized before it reaches the scorer.** The fraud system sees only token, BIN and last-4, which keeps it out of the cardholder-data environment (CDE) where possible. | A feature truly needs raw PAN (rare, since BIN covers most needs). That part then enters PCI scope with a separate CDE segment. |\n\n## 3. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n\n**The one real request:** a live production authorization goes from the auth switch to the scorer. The scorer returns `{decision, score, reason_codes, rule_version, model_version}`. It runs **inline but non-enforcing**: the switch logs our answer and keeps its own decision. This is the only safe way to get the real latency figure on day one.\n\n**Tiers crossed:**\n1. **Auth switch**: a new client call with a **30 ms hard timeout** and a circuit breaker, behind a feature flag with a traffic % dial (1% → 100%).\n2. **Scoring service** (gRPC, Kubernetes, 2 availability zones), with a minimal canonical request schema v0.\n3. **Online store** (Redis): read one feature, the card token's count of transactions in the last hour.\n4. **Decision**: one hard-coded velocity rule (e.g. more than 10 auths per hour means \"would decline\") and a constant model placeholder.\n5. **Event bus**: the decision event goes to Kafka through a non-blocking producer with a bounded local buffer, so the hot path never waits on Kafka.\n6. **Stream processor**: a Flink job consumes transaction events, updates the Redis velocity counter and sinks decisions to an Iceberg decision log.\n7. **Dashboard**: Grafana.\n\n**Deploy:** Terraform for infra. CI builds an image pinned by digest. GitOps (Argo CD) rolls it out. The switch flag starts at 1%.\n\n**Logged and monitored from day zero:**\n- An OpenTelemetry trace ID is carried from the switch through the scorer and Redis, into the Kafka header, and on to Flink.\n- Metrics: p50/p99/p99.9 latency, timeout rate, would-decline rate, Kafka consumer lag, and Redis error rate.\n- Alerts: p99 > 30 ms, timeout rate > 0.1%, would-decline rate moving ±3σ from baseline, consumer lag > 30 s.\n\n**Exit check:** 100% of production auths traverse the path. One transaction can be followed end to end in a single trace, from switch through scorer to Redis to Kafka to Flink to Iceberg. Real p99 is measured and confirmed under budget. AI layer\n**N/A as defined (no LLM, no agent).** This is a classical ML system, so the LLM-specific sublayers do not apply: prompt-injection defense, retrieval, LLM memory, orchestration and routing. Their ML equivalents are already in the plan:\n- Adversarial-input defense: tokenization, feature-validation defaults, rule kill switches (Phases 1, 2, 4).\n- Latency and cost budget: the 30 ms gate in Phase 0.\n- Human-in-the-loop: analyst review (Phase 6) and human model promotion (Phase 7).\n- Model access: in-process, swappable artifact (Phase 5).\n- Feedback: labels and retraining (Phases 3 and 7).\n\nThis section becomes active if the LLM analyst copilot in §7 is pulled forward.\n\n## 7. Deliberately deferred\n- **Graph and fraud-ring features (or a GNN).** Pull forward when ring or mule fraud exceeds about 15% of losses.\n- **Deep sequence models.** Pull forward when GBDT recall plateaus across two retrains and a shadow test shows material lift within budget.\n- **Online or continuous learning.** Pull forward when attack adaptation outpaces the daily retrain (loss spikes before the next model ships).\n- **Strongly consistent per-card counters.** Pull forward on the consistency gate's flip condition.\n- **Bought feature-store product (Feast/Tecton).** Pull forward when there are more than about 100 features or more than one team producing features.\n- **Self-serve rules UI for fraud ops.** Pull forward when rule changes exceed about 10 per week and pull-request review becomes the bottleneck.\n- **Exploration holdout** (letting a tiny, capped sample of would-be declines through to measure true outcomes). Pull forward when selection bias measurably distorts evaluation, and only with risk sign-off.\n- **LLM analyst copilot** (case summarization). Pull forward when analyst throughput is the binding constraint. This would activate the full AI layer in §6.\n- **More than 2 regions, and acquirer/merchant-side fraud.** Pull forward on new market entry or a product-scope change.\n\n## 8. Eval score: **19/20**\n\nI scored this myself, so an independent grader may score it lower.\n\n1. **Dependency ordering, 2/2.** Substrate → contracts → features and labels in parallel → rules → model → review → feedback loop → scale. No model work before features and labels exist.\n2. **Walking skeleton first, 2/2.** A real production auth crosses every tier, traced and alerted. It deliberately doesn't enforce decisions, because enforcing on day one would risk the worst failure.\n3. **Tradeoff gates, 2/2.** The four required gates plus failure mode, feature computation, model family, serving and PCI boundary.
